st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source materially extends the cluster’s call for continuous, use-specific evaluation by treating rubrics as part of the measurement system and providing a concrete discover–audit–repair framework across structural adequacy, reliability, preference fit and adversarial robustness. kp.k: Rubrics define the measurement, not merely scoring guidance
kp.d: This May 2026 arXiv paper studies open-ended AI evaluation rather than legal services directly. The authors treat the combination of a fixed judge and its rubric as the measurement instrument: changing rubric wording changes what response quality means operationally. They argue that plausible-sounding rubrics can reward fluent but unsupported responses, with reusable policy-level rubrics propagating such failures into evaluation, filtering and training.

kp.k: Trustworthy evaluation requires multiple distinct audit axes
kp.d: PReMISE audits structural adequacy, reliability, preference fit and adversarial robustness. Structural checks cover atomicity, internal consistency, observability, operationalizability and scope. Reliability probes measure agreement across judges, stochastic consistency and paraphrase stability. The authors distinguish these properties from predicting preferences and resisting gaming; strong agreement alone does not establish that a judge measures the intended quality.

kp.k: Discovery consolidates preference differences into reusable criteria
kp.d: The discovery pipeline extracts criteria distinguishing preferred and rejected responses, then embeds, clusters, subdivides and rewrites candidates into reusable criteria. A support filter and maximal marginal relevance selection balance source frequency and diversity. Consolidation is intended to preserve operationally distinct constructs. The UltraFeedback discovery trace reduces 3,151 candidates to 711 before filtering and selecting 20. Preference-oriented repair subsequently selects criteria aligned with the winning response rather than merely frequent differences.

kp.k: No evaluated rubric source leads every audit dimension
kp.d: The study compares PReMISE with Inverse CAI, Auto-Rubric, AutoRule, CritiQ and AgentEval across HH-RLHF, UltraFeedback, Arena-Expert-5K and HelpSteer3. It specifies 1,000 extraction pairs and a 500-pair audit pool per corpus. Table 1 reports AgentEval leading inter-judge agreement (α=.582) and paraphrase stability (.702), Auto-Rubric leading self-consistency (13.9% flip rate), VFR (.297) and preference accuracy (68.7%), and unconstrained PReMISE refinement leading structural adequacy (4.45 out of 5). Different measures therefore favour different sources.
qs: No source wins on all audit axes.
Six different rubric methods lead at least one col- umn; none leads them all.

kp.k: Preference coverage differs from aggregate predictive accuracy
kp.d: The authors distinguish applicability, source specificity and effective dimensionality from preference-prediction accuracy. On UltraFeedback, discovered PReMISE has .577 in-domain applicability, .502 out-of-domain applicability, 11.5 firing criteria per prompt and 15 effective dimensions across 20 criteria. AgentEval applies more broadly (.824) but has negative source specificity and only three effective dimensions; Auto-Rubric applies to .030 of prompts and has 10 effective dimensions. The authors characterise PReMISE as uniquely non-trivial on all three sub-axes, rather than universally best on each.

kp.k: Preference selection improves accuracy, conditional on judge capacity
kp.d: The headline reported mean preference accuracy rises from 65.0% to 68.6% after preference-rank selection across four corpora, three judges and two templates. Appendix B.4 separately reports a hierarchical aggregate improvement of +2.80 percentage points, CI [+2.04, +3.59], p<0.001. Evaluation uses majority-of-five sampling at temperature 0.7; the appendix specifies 3,000 pairs for UltraFeedback cells and other direct-verdict cells, but 1,000 for non-UltraFeedback per-rubric JSON cells. Repaired PReMISE leads or ties in four of six judge-template cells, but underperforms the no-rubric baseline on Qwen3-32B. These findings do not establish a universal advantage from supplying rubrics.

kp.k: Adversarial testing measures high-scoring, verified exploitation
kp.d: Verified Fool Rate counts attack responses that both score at least 7 on the stated 0–10 scale and receive an exploiting label from a separate automated verifier. The reported protocol uses Moonshot Kimi-K2-Thinking as attacker, DeepSeek-V3 as scoring judge, Mistral-Large-3 as verifier and 500 attacks per criterion. Attacks target rubric wording through strategies including false authority, formatting and irrelevant elaboration. The authors propose that operational specificity creates a precise attack surface; this is their explanation for discovered PReMISE's higher VFR than some broader or narrower baselines, not a demonstration that specificity is generally undesirable.

kp.k: Text refinement trades reliability against resistance to gaming
kp.d: The refinement process edits rubric wording using seven operators: applicability gates, do-not-reward clauses, score caps, decomposition, observable rewrites, false-positive anchors and non-compensation rules. Revisions face a structural budget and held-out acceptance tests. Reliability-constrained refinement reduces mean VFR from .464 to .360 while α falls from .531 to .519; unconstrained refinement reaches VFR .299 and α .488. Preference accuracy remains approximately unchanged at 64.9% and 64.8%, respectively. The constrained setting prohibits development-split α loss, but its reported evaluation still shows a small reliability decline.

kp.k: Human calibration supports, but limits, automated exploit labels
kp.d: The verifier validation uses 42 high-scoring samples: 25 attacker-generated and 17 baseline responses, spanning three corpora. Three human annotators provide majority labels, resulting in 19 exploiting and 23 genuine samples; six attacker-generated samples are judged genuine. Human agreement is α=.730. Against these labels, the automated verifier records TP=16, FP=6, FN=3 and TN=17, yielding precision 72.7%, recall 84.2% and F1 78.0%. VFR therefore remains an imperfect automated proxy rather than independently established ground truth.

kp.k: Scope and protocol qualifications limit downstream conclusions
kp.d: The authors limit the framework to preference-grounded policy rubrics, excluding objectives intended to override preferences such as hard safety constraints. They describe VFR as a protocol-dependent lower bound and acknowledge LLM mediation, source-data dependence and limited domain coverage. Downstream effects on reinforcement learning, data-quality measurement, judge improvement and response steering remain future work. The supplied document also contains protocol differences: Appendix B.1.4 describes a verifier blind to the targeted rubric, whereas the reproduced verifier prompt supplies the rubric and states that the response scored at least 7/10. The paper offers evaluation-methodology evidence, not observed changes in legal work or professional structures.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Roy and co-authors claim that reusable rubrics materially shape automated LLM evaluation, and that targeted rubric selection and editing can improve preference prediction or reduce susceptibility to gaming.
pts.d: This is a cross-domain source about LLM evaluation, not legal services. The authors treat a fixed model with different rubrics as different measurement instruments. They argue that plausible rubric wording can still induce scores that reward unsupported or otherwise unsuitable answers, and that agreement among judges does not establish validity or robustness. Their experiments find no rubric source that leads every audit dimension. They report that preference-aligned selection improves PReMISE's aggregate preference-prediction accuracy from 65.0% to 68.6%, while reliability-constrained refinement reduces Verified Fool Rate from 46.4% to 36.0%, with inter-judge agreement declining from α=.531 to .519. Unconstrained refinement reduces VFR further to .299 while agreement falls to .488. These are reported experimental findings rather than predictions of future occupational or market change.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The claims rest on comparative experiments across four preference datasets, six rubric-discovery methods, multiple LLM judges, adversarial testing, and a small human calibration study.
pts.d: The authors evaluate HH-RLHF, UltraFeedback, Arena-Expert-5K, and HelpSteer3, comparing PReMISE with Inverse CAI, Auto-Rubric, AutoRule, CritiQ, and AgentEval. They describe 1,000 discovery pairs and a 500-pair audit pool per dataset. Held-out preference evaluation uses three judges and two prompt templates, with majority voting over five samples at temperature 0.7. Appendix B.4 specifies 3,000 pairs per direct-verdict cell, but 1,000 for per-rubric JSON on the three non-UltraFeedback sources. The headline preference improvement is 3.6 percentage points; a separately reported hierarchical aggregate is +2.80 points, with a confidence interval of +2.04 to +3.59 and p<0.001. These summaries should remain distinct. Adversarial testing uses Kimi-K2-Thinking as attacker, DeepSeek-V3 as scoring judge, Mistral-Large-3 as verifier, a high-score threshold of 7/10, and 500 attempts per criterion. Human calibration involves 42 samples and three annotators, reporting verifier precision of 72.7%, recall of 84.2%, and F1 of 78.0%. The paper's automated verifier is an experimental classifier, not human verification of professional work.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The claims concern the paper's experimental setting, not a dated forecast; applicability depends on preference data, judge capacity, and the chosen attack and evaluation protocols.
pts.d: The supplied source is dated 29 May 2026. It gives no timeline for future adoption or legal-market effects. Its scope is reusable policy-level rubrics derived from or assessed against pairwise preferences, excluding objectives intended to override preferences, such as hard safety constraints. The authors qualify the results by judge capacity: preference-repaired PReMISE performs below the no-rubric baseline on Qwen3-32B. They characterize VFR as a protocol-specific lower bound on exploitability and absolute measurements as judge-relative because the pipeline is LLM-mediated. Discovery is bounded by the source data's annotation protocol, label density, and polarization. The constrained repair permits no development-split α loss, but reported evaluation agreement nevertheless decreases slightly. Broader domains, downstream training and deployment effects, multilingual applications, and modality-specific extensions remain future work.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The affected actors are designers and operators of LLM evaluation, benchmark, filtering, and training systems, rather than any identified legal-service segment.
pts.d: The authors argue that rubric reuse makes specification flaws consequential across many evaluations. Their proposed discover–audit–repair workflow gives evaluation researchers and system operators separate ways to improve preference fit and adversarial robustness, rather than a universally superior rubric. Operators must choose between reliability and robustness depending on whether a rubric acts as a passive scorer or an active optimization or selection target. Users of systems evaluated this way are indirectly implicated by whether scoring rewards genuine quality or superficial gaming, but the paper does not measure downstream user outcomes. It makes no specific claims about lawyers, clients, law firms, legal employment, pricing, or access to justice.
